title: Cervical Myelopathy
case: Case: A 63-year-old man reports six months of dropping things and walking unsteadily. Both hands are numb. Hoffmann sign is positive bilaterally, gait is wide-based, and reflexes in the legs are brisk. He has no bladder change.

Working diagnosis: suspected cervical myelopathy. Action: urgent referral to a spine surgeon or neurologist for imaging. No cervical manipulation, traction or compression testing. Document baseline measures.
qa: Why is neck pain not required for the diagnosis? Because the cord can be compressed without much pain. Hand and gait signs are the main clues.
Why avoid traction here? It may change the position of structures around the cord, and benefit is not established. The safer decision is to avoid it until a physician has reviewed the imaging.

The patient has only one positive Hoffmann sign and normal gait. What now? One sign has limited value alone. Complete the UMN screen. If other signs are present, refer. If all others are normal, document and monitor, with a clear plan to re-test.
Why document baseline gait and grip? So that change over time can be recognised and communicated to the physician.
A patient starts to lose bladder control with these signs. What urgency? Emergency. It suggests advanced cord involvement.

fields.Purpose: Screen for UMN involvement in the upper limb
fields.Patient position: Sitting, hand relaxed with the fingers slightly flexed
fields.Therapist position: In front, holding the patient's middle finger
fields.Action: Hold the middle finger at the middle phalanx. Quickly flick the fingernail of the middle finger downward so the fingertip snaps
fields.Positive: Involuntary flexion of the thumb and index finger
fields.Supports: UMN pathway involvement; supports further assessment
fields.Limits: Can be present in some people without disease; not specific to cord compression alone [Ref – to verify]
fields.Common errors: Flicking too softly; patient's hand tense or held rigid
fields.Next step: If positive, complete the rest of the UMN screen and consider referral

fields.Purpose: Screen for UMN involvement in the lower limb
fields.Action: Stroke firmly along the outer edge of the sole from the heel toward the toes, then curve across the ball of the foot
fields.Positive: Great toe extends (goes up), other toes may fan
fields.Error: Stroking too lightly or causing a withdrawal reflex

fields.Action: Tap the brachioradialis tendon at the distal radius
fields.Positive: Finger flexion with little or no forearm movement; sometimes with shoulder flexion
fields.Meaning: Suggests a lesion at the C5–C6 level with UMN involvement. Interpret within the cluster [Ref – to verify]

fields.Action: Support the knee slightly flexed; quickly dorsiflex the ankle and hold light pressure
fields.Positive: Rhythmic repeated beats of the foot

fields.Action: The patient makes a fist and opens it fully, as fast as possible, for 10 seconds, with the arm held in front
fields.Positive: Slow or incomplete cycles compared with normal reference values [Ref – to verify]

redFlags.Finding: Rapidly worsening weakness, gait or hand function
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop the session, document, arrange transfer to emergency or spine service

redFlags.Finding: Bladder or bowel change with new limb signs
Acute neck trauma plus neurological signs
Stable but clear UMN signs with no rapid change
redFlags.Why it matters: Compression likely but not rapidly worsening
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop neck loading, refer to spine surgeon or neurologist

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: none to the neck. Do not apply cervical manipulation, traction, strong mobilization or end-range techniques while cord compression is suspected. The risk may outweigh any benefit [Ref – to verify]. Gentle thoracic and shoulder girdle work may be considered only after medical clearance and when it does not provoke cord symptoms.

exercise.Situation: Mild stable myelopathy managed non-surgically by the medical team
exercise.Approach: Supervised program agreed with the team: gait and balance training, hand dexterity, gentle general conditioning, fall-prevention advice. Avoid end-range neck loading
Follow the surgeon's protocol: early walking, gradual range, hand and gait retraining, progressive strengthening as cleared

exerciseNotes: Before medical assessment, do not start a strengthening program. After physician review:

Example progression logic: if gait stays stable and no new symptoms appear for the review period, increase walking time and balance difficulty gradually. If any new weakness, hand deterioration or bladder change appears, stop and refer. These are illustrations, not a protocol.
modalityNotes: Not indicated as a primary treatment. They do not change cord compression. If the patient is awaiting review, avoid heat or electrical applications that mask worsening sensory change.
pathway: Any emergency red flag? Yes: emergency action.
Hand clumsiness, gait change, or UMN signs? Yes: working diagnosis is suspected cervical myelopathy. Go to step 3.
Is the change rapid? Yes: urgent same-day review. No: urgent referral within days.
Document findings (gait, hand function, reflexes, UMN signs) so the physician sees the baseline.

Supports: hand clumsiness, bilateral signs, gait change, Hoffmann, Babinski, hyperreflexia. Argues against: purely unilateral radicular pattern with normal gait and reflexes. Must not miss: progressive compression, tumour, infection.
Refer using the urgency level from Section G.
Educate: explain that the neck needs medical imaging, avoid risky activities and falls, report any sudden worsening.
